newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: Saudi plans shake-up of electricity sector.
newsitem.headline: Saudi plans shake-up of electricity sector.

text.p: Saudi Arabia plans major changes to its electricity sector to keep pace with domestic power demand, Saudi Minister of Industry and Electricity Hashem bin Abdullah bin Hashem Yamani said on Tuesday.

Riyadh's plans to the year 2020 call for a near quadrupling in generating capacity, an increased role for foreign private finance, restructured state power firms, partial removal of price subsidies and greater use of gas, Yamani said.
"Extending the electrical generating capacity and distribution capacity is of utmost priority," Yamani told industry delegates at the Gulf 97 conference in Abu Dhabi.
Saudi Arabia is already struggling to keep pace with surging electricity demand and has had on occassions in the past three years experienced black-outs in some cities during load times.

The cost of meeting 4.5 percent annual average electricity demand growth called for a total investment of 438 billion Saudi riyals ($117 billion) in order to boost generating capacity to 69,520-megawatts (MW) in 2020 from 19,662 MW in 1995.
Some 237 billion riyals were needed to be invested in power generation, 126 billion riyals for transmission and 75 billion riyals for the distribution network.

Saudi electricity demand, spurred by an expected doubling of the population over 25 years and growing residential and commercial use, would total 59,267 MW in 2020 from 19,573 MW in 1995, Yamani told delegates.

Large-scale investments required to meet this demand would open up the domestic power sector to foreign investment and lead, in Yamani's words, to a "unbundling" of the four power utilities Saudi Consolidated Electric Power Company (SCECOs).
SCECOs would eventually be broken up into generation, transmission and distribution "separate entities" which would be open to private investors, Yamani said.

"To speed up the sector...(it is planned) to unbundle power firms in Saudi Arabia into generation, transmission and distribution sectors and to open (these) sectors to all forms of participation by the international private sector, financial or management," Yamani told delegates.
"The basic motivation is not to look at privatisation like a dogma...Mostly it (private finance) is going to be in new projects," he said.
The domestic state-subsidised tariff structure would also be "restructured" in an attempt to attract foreign investment.
"Tariffs will have to change to provide enough to finance these tremendous expansions...But the changes in the tariff schedule are not as big as people may fear," he said.

Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil producer and exporter, is trying to diversify its economy, lessen dependence on state spending and move away from a generous welfare system where most basic utilities are heavily subsidised.

Foreign firms are working at a $1.7 billion, 1,286 MW power plant in Riyadh which started in November as part of the 25-year development plan and a tender to construct a 1,750 MW plant at Shuaiba is also underway.
Gas reserves were also planned to be developed, particularly in the central region, to meet rising power demand, Yamani said.
"Our real desire is to see gas in Saudi Arabia be available not just in the Eastern province but other regions," he said.
